prompt: Why can no part of an IPv4 address be larger than 255?
hint: Each part is a fixed number of bits.

choices.text: Anything above that value is reserved for the private ranges instead
choices.why: Private ranges are ordinary values; they are not above the ceiling.

choices.text: Each of the four parts is eight bits, and eight bits count to 255
choices.why: The address is thirty-two bits written as four bytes.

choices.text: The designers picked a round limit that was easy to remember
choices.why: The limit is arithmetic rather than a choice about memorability.

choices.text: Routers are built to hold a number of that width and would ignore the rest
choices.why: Routers store far larger numbers; the constraint is the width of the field.

prompt: Your machine shows `192.168.1.24`. What does a server on the internet see as your address?
hint: That range never leaves a local network.

choices.text: The same address, since that is the one the machine was actually given
choices.why: Nothing on the internet routes to `192.168.x.x`, so it cannot be that.

choices.text: Your household's single public address, shared with everything in it
choices.why: A private address is never routed, so something rewrites it on the way out.

choices.text: No address back, since a private one has no route out to the internet
choices.why: They reach it perfectly well; the address is translated first.

choices.text: A different private address, chosen for you by your provider's equipment
choices.why: What the server sees has to be routable, which a private address is not.

prompt: Fill the blank: `127.0.0.1` is the ___ address, which never reaches a network card at all.
hint: It is what `localhost` resolves to.

prompt: Which of these ranges are private? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three ranges were set aside on purpose.

choices.why: Sixteen million addresses, common in companies and cloud networks.
The one almost every home router uses.
An ordinary public range, reserved only for use in documentation.
A million addresses, often seen around containers.
That is loopback, which is a different kind of reservation.

prompt: A range of 256 addresses gives 254 usable ones. What are the other two?
hint: Neither of them can belong to a machine.

choices.text: The first names the network itself and the last is broadcast
choices.why: Neither can be assigned, which is where the subtraction comes from.

choices.text: The first and last are reserved for the gateway and the DNS server
choices.why: Both are ordinary addresses given to ordinary machines.

choices.text: They are the loopback and the unspecified address
choices.why: Those live in ranges of their own, not inside each network.

choices.text: They are held back in case the range has to grow
choices.why: A range does not grow; its size is fixed by the mask.

prompt: What question does the mask answer?
hint: It is asked once per packet sent.

choices.text: Which of the addresses around it are private and which ones are public
choices.why: That is decided by the range, not by the mask.

choices.text: How many machines this particular network is allowed to hold
choices.why: That follows from the mask, but it is not the question being asked.

choices.text: Which address on this wire belongs to which network card
choices.why: That is ARP, and it happens after the mask has answered.

choices.text: Which addresses are on my own wire and which go to the gateway
choices.why: The first decision in routing, made on every packet.

prompt: How many usable addresses does a `/26` network hold?
hint: Six host bits, and two addresses are not usable.

prompt: A machine at `192.168.1.24/24` sends to `192.168.2.99`. What does it do?
hint: Compare the network parts.

choices.text: Refuses to send, because the two sit in different private ranges
choices.why: They are on the same private range, and different networks within it.

choices.text: Hands the packet to its gateway, because the network parts differ
choices.why: With `/24` the first three numbers are the network, and they do not match.

choices.text: Sends the frame straight there, because both start with `192.168`
choices.why: `/24` makes the third number part of the network too.

choices.text: Asks the wire for the destination's MAC and sends the frame directly
choices.why: That happens only for a local address, and this one is not.

prompt: A machine has the right address and a mask that is too wide. What is the symptom?
hint: It will treat some distant machines as local.

choices.text: It is refused an address of its own when it tries to join the network
choices.why: The address is fine; it is how the machine reads it that is wrong.

choices.text: It reaches some machines and not others, with no pattern that makes sense
choices.why: It shouts on its own wire for machines that are not on it.

choices.text: It reaches what it should, though a good deal more slowly than before
choices.why: The failures are total for the affected destinations rather than slow.

choices.text: It stops reaching anything it needs, whether near or distant
choices.why: Local traffic keeps working, which is what makes this confusing.

prompt: Fill the blank: every extra bit given to the network part ___ the number of addresses in the range.
hint: From 256 to 128 to 64.

prompt: How many bits is an IPv6 address?
hint: Four times the IPv4 width.

choices.text: 64 bits, which is half of it
choices.why: That is the size of the network part in a common allocation, not the address.

choices.text: 32 bits, as in the older one
choices.why: That is IPv4, which is what ran out.
Which is 2⁹⁶ times as many addresses, not four times.

choices.text: 256 bits, twice the true width
choices.why: Larger than needed and not the figure chosen.

prompt: Why may `::` appear only once in an IPv6 address?
hint: It stands for a run of something.

choices.text: Writing it twice over would make the address longer than its own 128 bits
choices.why: Shortening never changes the value, only how it is written.

choices.text: Two of them would leave no way to tell how many zero groups each replaced
choices.why: The shortening is only reversible while there is one gap to fill.

choices.text: By convention it is the first run of zeros that gets omitted
choices.why: It is not a convention about which run; it is that one is reversible and two are not.

choices.text: The notation keeps the second one for writing the port number
choices.why: A port is written elsewhere, in brackets, and is unrelated.

prompt: Why does IPv6 remove the need for NAT?
hint: Ask what NAT was working around.

choices.text: There are enough addresses for every device to have a globally unique one
choices.why: Sharing one public address between a household stops being necessary.

choices.text: An IPv6 header is not something a router may rewrite in transit
choices.why: They could be; the point is that there is no reason to.

choices.text: It carries the private address along inside the public one it was given
choices.why: There are no private addresses to carry.

choices.text: Routers along the path refuse to translate an IPv6 address
choices.why: Nothing refuses it; it is simply unnecessary.

prompt: Why has IPv6 taken so long to be adopted? Choose all that apply.
hint: One fact about the two protocols explains most of it.

choices.text: NAT made the shortage bearable for long enough
choices.why: The pressure that would have forced the change was relieved.

choices.text: The specification itself was finished fairly recently
choices.why: It was finished in 1998.

choices.text: IPv6 turns out to be rather slower than IPv4 once it is put into practice
choices.why: It is not; the header is simpler and there is no translation.

choices.text: Nobody can switch until everybody has, so both run at once
choices.why: Which is dual stack, and is where most of the internet is.

choices.text: An IPv6-only machine cannot talk to an IPv4-only server at all
choices.why: The addresses do not fit in each other's headers.

prompt: Fill the blank: an IPv6 address beginning `fe80:` is ___-local, valid on this wire only and never routed.
hint: The machine generates it without asking anybody.

prompt: A laptop moves from home to an office to another country. What changes?
hint: One address belongs to the network and the other to the hardware.

choices.text: Its MAC address changes each time and its IP address does not
choices.why: That is the two the other way round.

choices.text: Its IP address changes each time and its MAC address does not
choices.why: One says where in the world; the other says which card.

choices.text: Neither of them changes, since it is the same machine throughout
choices.why: The IP is given by whichever network it joined.

choices.text: Both change, since it joined a different network each time
choices.why: The MAC belongs to the card, not to the network it is on.

prompt: Why can a router hold one line for a million IP addresses, but nothing equivalent for MAC addresses?
hint: One of the two has structure.

choices.text: MAC addresses are the longer of the two, so they take up far too much room
choices.why: Six bytes against four; length is not the obstacle.

choices.text: Routers along the path are not permitted to read a MAC address
choices.why: They read them constantly; they cannot summarise them.

choices.text: An IP address splits into a network part and a host part; a MAC does not
choices.why: There is no network of MACs to summarise.

choices.text: MAC addresses change far too often for a table to be worth keeping
choices.why: They change less than IP addresses do, not more.

prompt: What is `ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff`?
hint: Every card on the wire accepts it.

choices.text: The broadcast address — every card on the wire takes the frame
choices.why: It is how a machine asks a question before it knows who to ask.

choices.text: A multicast group that devices on the wire may opt into
choices.why: Multicast is a group; this is everybody, with no opting.

choices.text: A card that has not yet been given an address of its own by anybody
choices.why: A card's address is burned in; it is never absent.

choices.text: An address held in reserve for whichever card is the gateway
choices.why: A gateway has an ordinary card with an ordinary address.

prompt: Why do phones invent a different MAC address for each Wi-Fi network they join?
hint: The number is stable, and that is the problem.

choices.text: Two of the networks would otherwise hand them the very same address
choices.why: Addresses on different networks do not collide; they are never compared.

choices.text: It speeds up the connection between the phone and the access point
choices.why: It has no effect on speed at all.

choices.text: A stable number lets a network recognise the same device across visits
choices.why: Changing it per network is a defence against being tracked.

choices.text: It is required before a network will hand out an IP address
choices.why: Nothing requires it; it is a deliberate privacy measure.

prompt: Match each kind of frame destination to what it means.
hint: One of them is a group that devices opt into.

pairs.right: One specific card, which is nearly all traffic
Every card on the wire accepts it
A group — cards that opted in accept it, the rest do not

right_distractors: The gateway, whichever card that happens to be
Whichever card replies to the question first

prompt: A machine needs to send a frame to a local address it has never spoken to. What does it do first?
hint: There is no directory to consult.

choices.text: Broadcasts a question to the whole wire asking who holds that address
choices.why: Only the machine that recognises it replies, and it replies directly.

choices.text: Asks the DHCP server, since that is what handed the address out
choices.why: DHCP hands out addresses and is not consulted afterwards.

choices.text: Asks its gateway to supply that machine's MAC address for it
choices.why: The gateway is not involved in local traffic and keeps no such list.

choices.text: Sends the frame off to the broadcast address and lets it find its own way
choices.why: The packet would arrive everywhere, which is not how the frame is addressed.

prompt: Why is the very first packet to a machine you have not spoken to recently slower?
hint: Something has to happen before the frame can be built.

choices.text: There is a broadcast and a reply before the frame can be addressed
choices.why: A millisecond, and the reason a first attempt is never the one to measure.

choices.text: The connection has to be agreed with the far end before data is sent
choices.why: That is the TCP handshake, which is a different delay in a different place.

choices.text: The routing table may have to be searched through for the first time
choices.why: The table is searched for every packet, not only the first.

choices.text: The name has to be looked up before the address is known
choices.why: That is DNS, and it happens before any of this.

prompt: Any machine on a wire can answer an ARP question claiming to be the gateway. Why is that possible?
hint: Ask what could do the verifying.

choices.text: The gateway itself does not answer ARP questions about its own address
choices.why: It answers normally; the attacker simply answers first or more often.

choices.text: Cards are allowed to share a MAC address on the same wire
choices.why: They are not, and that is a different problem.

choices.text: ARP has no authentication, and the first answer is believed
choices.why: There is nothing on a local network that could verify the claim.

choices.text: The question is sent before the asking machine has an address of its own
choices.why: The asker has an address; that is not what is missing.

prompt: Fill the two blanks: the ARP question goes to ___, and the answer goes to ___.
hint: One is the whole wire and one is a single machine.

prompt: Why does a machine that has just been given an address ask about its own address?
hint: It is not expecting an answer.

choices.text: To confirm with the DHCP server that the lease was granted
choices.why: The lease was already acknowledged; ARP is not part of that.

choices.text: Because a frame stays unbuildable until it has asked at least once
choices.why: It could build frames immediately; this is an announcement.

choices.text: So everything updates its cache, and so a reply would reveal a duplicate
choices.why: Which is how two machines on one address complain rather than fail silently.

choices.text: To find out which of the gateways on the wire it should be using
choices.why: The gateway arrived with the lease, not from ARP.

prompt: Put the four steps of getting an address in order.
hint: It begins with a machine that has no address at all.
items: The new machine asks whether anybody hands out addresses
The machine says it will take that one
The server acknowledges, with a length of time attached
trap: The common swap is putting the acknowledgement before the request — the server does not commit an address until the machine has said it wants that one, because several servers may have offered.

prompt: A machine shows an address in `169.254.x.x`. What does that mean?
hint: Something did not happen.

choices.text: It has been given a private address by the router
choices.why: A router hands out its own private range; this one it gave itself.

choices.text: Its lease has expired and is being renewed
choices.why: During renewal it keeps using the address it had.

choices.text: Nothing answered its request for an address
choices.why: The machine gave itself one, which points at the cable, the association or the server.

choices.text: It has been refused access to the network on purpose
choices.why: A refusal is an answer; this is the absence of one.

prompt: What arrives along with the address? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three other settings, and the failures live in them.

choices.text: A DNS server
choices.why: Where name lookups go.

choices.text: The mask
choices.why: Which decides what counts as local.

choices.text: The MAC address of the router
choices.why: That is discovered by ARP when it is needed, not handed over.

choices.text: The public address of the household
choices.why: The machine never learns it; only the router uses it.

choices.text: The gateway
choices.why: The last line of the routing table.

prompt: A printer worked yesterday and cannot be found today, and nothing was reconfigured. What is the likely cause?
hint: An address is lent, not given.

choices.text: Its lease expired and it came back with a different address
choices.why: Whatever was pointing at the old one still is.

choices.text: Its MAC address changed when it restarted
choices.why: A MAC belongs to the card and does not change on a restart.

choices.text: The DHCP server refused to give it an address this time
choices.why: Then it would have no address at all rather than a different one.

choices.text: The mask configured on that whole network was changed by somebody
choices.why: That would affect every device, not one printer.

prompt: Somebody plugs a home router into an office wall socket. Some machines then work perfectly and others do not, with no pattern. Why?
hint: Two servers are now answering the same question.

choices.text: The office network has now run out of addresses to hand out
choices.why: A second server adds addresses rather than exhausting them.

choices.text: The new router blocks any of the traffic that it does not itself recognise
choices.why: The machines that took its offer reach it fine; they simply go nowhere.

choices.text: The two routers fight over the same address and both stop
choices.why: Neither stops; both keep answering, which is the problem.

choices.text: Each machine takes the first offer it receives, and now there are two
choices.why: Half get the right settings and half get a gateway pointing at a home router.

prompt: Match each address to what it is.
hint: Two of them can never belong to a machine.

pairs.right: The name of a network rather than anything in it
A machine that asked for an address and got no answer

right_distractors: A public address routable from anywhere
The gateway of a home network

prompt: How many usable addresses does a `/30` network hold?
hint: It is the size used between two routers.

prompt: Which of these is decided by the mask rather than by the address?
hint: One question is asked per packet sent.

choices.text: Which network card the frame is addressed to
choices.why: That is ARP, after the mask has answered.

choices.text: Whether an address is private or public
choices.why: That is the range the address falls in.

choices.text: Whether a destination is on my own wire
choices.why: Compare the network parts; identical means local.

choices.text: Which server hands out addresses here
choices.why: That is DHCP, and nothing about the mask says it.

prompt: Put in order what happens when a machine sends to a local address it has not met.
hint: Two of the steps are about a different layer from the others.
items: The mask says the destination is on this wire
The ARP cache is checked and has no entry
A question goes to the broadcast address
The holder of the address replies with its MAC
The frame is built and sent
trap: The common swap is asking the wire before checking the mask — a machine that has not decided the destination is local has no reason to ask anybody on this wire about it.

prompt: A machine has a valid address and mask, can reach other machines on its own network, and can reach nothing beyond it. What is wrong?
hint: Three settings arrive with an address.

choices.text: Its ARP cache has gone stale and holds the wrong pairings
choices.why: A stale entry affects one destination, not everything beyond the network.

choices.text: Its mask is too narrow for the network it is sitting on
choices.why: A narrow mask breaks local traffic, and local traffic works.

choices.text: The gateway it was handed is wrong or not answering
choices.why: Local traffic never consults it, which is why only distant traffic fails.

choices.text: Its DNS server is not answering
choices.why: That breaks names and leaves addresses working; here nothing distant works.

prompt: Fill the two blanks: the ___ address says where in the world, and the ___ address says which card on this wire.
hint: One is given by the network, one by the factory.

prompt: Why does a private address not cause a conflict when millions of houses use the same one?
hint: Ask where such a packet is allowed to go.

choices.text: Nothing on the internet routes to it, so the two never meet
choices.why: The address is meaningful only within one local network.

choices.text: The router renumbers them before they are used
choices.why: They are used as they are and translated only on the way out.

choices.text: Private addresses are checked for uniqueness when assigned
choices.why: They are checked within one network and nowhere wider.

choices.text: Each household is given a different slice of the private range
choices.why: They are not; the same range is reused everywhere.

prompt: Which of these trust whoever answers first? Choose all that apply.
hint: Both were designed for a wire nobody expected to be hostile.

choices.text: DHCP
choices.why: A second server on a network hands out its own settings.

choices.text: The mask on a machine
choices.why: It is a configured value, not an answer from anybody.

choices.text: The routing table on a router
choices.why: It is a table the router keeps, not a question it asks the wire.

choices.text: A frame's checksum
choices.why: It is computed rather than claimed.

choices.text: ARP
choices.why: Any machine can claim to hold any address.

prompt: NAT is sometimes called a firewall. What is true about that?
hint: Ask what happens to an unsolicited packet arriving from outside.

choices.text: It refuses inbound connections as a side effect, without being designed to
choices.why: There is no table row to rewrite, so the packet has nowhere to go.

choices.text: It blocks outbound connections unless some rule explicitly allows them
choices.why: Outbound is exactly what creates the table row.

choices.text: It was designed as a firewall and address sharing came later
choices.why: It was designed to share addresses; the refusal is accidental.

choices.text: It inspects the traffic passing through it and blocks what looks dangerous
choices.why: It inspects nothing; it rewrites two numbers and looks up a table.

prompt: Why does NAT need to rewrite the port as well as the address?
hint: Thirty devices share one address.

choices.text: The original port number is not valid once it leaves the local network
choices.why: A port is a number with no local or public meaning.

choices.text: The port numbers have to match at both ends of a given connection
choices.why: They routinely differ; that is what a source port is for.

choices.text: It prevents two machines choosing the same private address
choices.why: Addresses are kept distinct by DHCP, not by NAT.

choices.text: The port is what tells the thirty devices behind one address apart
choices.why: The table maps a public port back to one machine and its own port.

prompt: Fill the two blanks: what DHCP hands out is ___ rather than given, which is why a device that was switched off for a week can come back with a different ___.
hint: The first word appears in the DHCP acknowledgement.

prompt: Why does a machine have two addresses rather than one?
hint: They answer different questions.

choices.text: One says where in the world it is and the other says which card it is
choices.why: A card that kept one worldwide address as it moved could not be routed to.

choices.text: One of the two is used for IPv4 and the other one of them for IPv6
choices.why: Those are both IP addresses; the MAC is a different kind.

choices.text: One is for sending and the other is for receiving
choices.why: Both are used in both directions.

choices.text: One of the two is public and the other one is private
choices.why: Those are both IP addresses too.
